essence: Every task carries an expected outcome (set before it starts) and a complete 0-1 (percentage of complete subtasks when it has subtasks); tasks render() their own View, have an on-demand tasks List, carry git commit refs, a priority, and are registered to a session but may live in a module or on a page. AITask and AISession should use this Task, not be Pages. This task system is the mechanism that tracks progress, so sessions piggyback on their tasks.

Three Task.replay rules miscount tasks (found by Server/State.mjs's self-check, exact edits in Server/doc/state.md "Decision"): (1) replay_line reads `at` but the item tool stamps `ts`, so completed_at falls back to the wall clock — use `line.at ?? line.ts ?? …`; (2) replay_legacy needs a non-empty outcome besides landed_at, so 33 landed session tasks replay as running; (3) complete() refuses a recorded finish while a {task: ref} child the worker merely filed is idle (sheet-handoff-proof, 10-17) — don't refuse during replay (this._rp set). State works around (1) on input only; (2) and (3) stay visible as the check's red line until Task.js is edited.

outcome.note: Three Task.replay rules fixed in Task.js (ts, landed_at alone, finish stands after a filed child); State check green, landed today 45 = 45. Merged from worktree/task-rules.

essence: Later, with a shape discussion the owner signs off before any build: moving a task out of a session's prompt into the module it concerns, for example to query all of a page's tasks. Use an item "move with a back reference" (the lines move, nothing is duplicated, and the session keeps a pointer for its cost and completion). Avoid littering modules with thousands of micro tasks; quick fixes may live there as single tasks, and every commit touching a module could be logged on its page. Open questions: is the moved task a record of "what changed" or a live AI task with subtasks and cost, and how do costs roll up across the move?

essence: The owner, 2026-10-25, reading session e00f55c9's numbers. (1) The completion numbers are confusing because they count different sets. progress() and completion count only DIRECT tasks, and leave stopped ones out of the total. rates() walks EVERY depth, owner asks separately, and leaves only "fair" stops out. One summary should say plainly which set each number counts, or use a single set. (2) The 20% red line (Task.RATES.red) was the tab's guess, not the owner's rule, and needs the owner's sign-off. (3) A high deferral count is a smell: it may mean tasks were made that were never really asked for (an AI offshoot). Or it may be a real triage pass: capture every ask first, then decide later which to drop. Make that second pass explicit, and flag deferred tasks that don't trace back to the owner's own words.

The owner, 2026-10-25, session e00f55c9-bad4-4ee2-899e-d629ea1eede6, which ended at 56% complete with 223 top-level tasks undone. (1) Every state needs a plain, written definition the owner can read: complete, stopped, "fair" stop, waiting, deferred, idle and running. The owner thought "deferred" meant "decided not to do". (2) Deferral should have levels instead of one flag: queued for later at medium or low priority; very low (may never get done); and floated but not queued at all. Each level is shown and counted on its own. (3) The owner's concern: a session that closes with hundreds of open tasks will forget them once everyone moves on. Open work must be prioritised and carried somewhere a later session will see it, not left under waiting records. (4) Review this session: what was asked, what was done, what is still to do. Ask the owner before spending on it; the week is over pace.
